title: Arts analogy: nested ends toward the commonwealth; necessity, order, harmony referred to power, wisdom, love
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Freedom altogether stands as in ye one God alone. order to wisdom, plus ye harmony belonging toward ye better to love — all things happen necessarily out from a certain coercion, either pure or mixed with love, or else altogether free — and because whatever happens necessarily stands as so ordered that same it happens toward ye better — as necessity stands as referred to power. Of ye extrinsic it stands as plain that same it stands as God Himself. speaking belonging toward ye intrinsic good — but we mean that same toward ye sake belonging toward that same which order is. Hence Aristotle too thinks ye good belonging toward ye universe stands as order; but belonging toward trade plus belonging toward all ye other arts together ye commonwealth cares, because its happiness consists in their communication — of ye merchandise ye merchant cares. but that same he may finish his voyage; — the sailor does not ask whether ye wares stand as good or useless. insofar as he stands as hired by means belonging toward another, does not look to that same further end but has his own; — he who builds a ship toward navigation. while he himself looks to his wage — that stands as understood by means belonging toward ye one who hired him. He who hews does not understand ye building; but that same by means belonging toward such labor he may seek his living — for ye cutter belonging toward timber does not cut so that same it may be hewn. coexistence, plus compact, we see some to be ends belonging toward others — as ye end belonging toward navigation stands as merchandise, belonging toward shipbuilding navigation, belonging toward hewing timber shipbuilding, belonging toward cutting hewing — plus yet these arts do not communicate among themselves — yet because all things stand as bound together by means belonging toward place.
pass_b_english: Yet because all things are bound together by place, coexistence, and compact, we see some to be ends of others — as the end of navigation is merchandise, of shipbuilding navigation, of hewing timber shipbuilding, of cutting hewing — and yet these arts do not communicate among themselves. For the cutter of timber does not cut so that it may be hewn, but that by such labor he may seek his living. He who hews does not understand the building; that is understood by the one who hired him, while he himself looks to his wage. He who builds a ship for navigation, insofar as he is hired by another, does not look to that further end but has his own; the sailor does not ask whether the wares are good or useless, but that he may finish his voyage; of the merchandise the merchant cares, but of trade and of all the other arts together the commonwealth cares, because its happiness consists in their communication.

Hence Aristotle too thinks the good of the universe is order; but we mean that for the sake of which order is, speaking of the intrinsic good. Of the extrinsic it is plain that it is God Himself. And because whatever happens necessarily is so ordered that it happens for the better — as necessity is referred to power, order to wisdom, and the harmony of the better to love — all things happen necessarily from a certain coercion, either pure or mixed with love, or else altogether free. Freedom altogether is in the one God alone.
source_text: At quia res omnes colligatae sunt loco et coexistentia et compactu, videmus alias aliarum esse fines, sicuti navigationis finis est mercatura, fabricationis navis finis est navigatio, dolationis lignorum est fabricatio, sectionis dolatio, et tamen hae artes inter se non communicant. Nam sector lignorum non secat ut dolentur, sed ut tali labore ipse victum quaerat. Qui vero dolat, non fabricationem intelligit, sed ea ab eo intelligitur qui eum conduxit, ipse vero mercedem intuetur. Qui navim fabricat ad navigationem, quatenus ab alio est non respicit, sed suum habet finem; nauta vero non respicit utrum merces bonae an inutiles sint, sed ut conficiat suum iter; de mercimonio enim curat mercator, de mercatura vero deque omnibus artibus caeteris simul curat respublica, quoniam in illarum communicatione eius consistit felicitas. Unde et Aristoteles bonum universi putat esse ordinem; sed nos id propter quod est ordo loquendo de bono intrinseco. Nam de extrinseco patet quod sit ipse Deus. Quoniam vero quaecunque necessario eveniunt ea ita ordinata sunt ut propter melius eveniant, prout necessitas ad potentiam, ordo ad sapientiam, harmonia melioris ad amorem referuntur. Eveniunt autem necessario omnia ex coactione quodammodo, eaque aut pura aut mixta amori, vel omnino libera. Libertas autem omnino in ipso uno Deo.
